text:
The ship's pool deck was the size of a city block, and every man on it seemed to know my father.

Four hundred guests had booked the Meridian for the week of June tenth, and the brochure that arrived at his apartment in May, glossy, laminated, smelling faintly of vanilla, had promised a "celebration of queer joy" and, in smaller print, "family-friendly programming." I was sixteen. I had spent my entire life inside my father's world, and this was the first time that world had gotten on a boat. This happened two years ago. I want to tell it the way it happened, which is to say in a jumble, because it happened in a jumble.

My father came home from the bar every night with a different story and the same shirt. The bar was called the Porch, and it was on the strip, and I worked the register there from the age of fourteen until I was sixteen, because Sunny, the manager, had known my father since the nineties and decided the daughter of the house should be trained before the house could be trusted with her. The Porch had red stools, a jukebox that skipped on certain songs, and a clientele that ranged from retired dentists to twenty-somethings who had moved from three different cities to end up at the same bar. Benny was a dentist. Ray was a former accountant who brought my father soup in a thermos when he got sick. Marcus had met my father at a Pride parade in 2009 and wore cargo shorts regardless of season. I learned all of this before I learned much else about anything, because the Porch was where I did my homework and where I ate lunch on school days and where, by eleven, I could tell you who was married to whom, who was saving for a second trip to Europe, and who had stopped coming in after his wife's brother died.

I was raised, in effect, by a chorus of men who were mostly done being raised by the world. They were not cruel to me. They were the opposite of cruel, which turned out to be harder to manage. When I was small they put me on their laps at the bar and asked me to guess who would win the World Series. When I was nine they braided my hair at the Sunday brunch, which required a dress code and a dessert that Sunny called the pride cake and that tasted like frosting and disappointment. When I was twelve they asked me, all of them, separately, whether I was gay, and when I said I didn't know, they all said, "Good, you've got time," and I have spent my whole life trying to figure out whether that was a gift or a verdict.

The first boy I ever brought home was in ninth grade. His name was Josh, and he was kind, and he asked me, gently, whether my father had a boyfriend, and I heard my own voice say no, which was true and also a lie, and he looked at me the way you look at someone who has just said something slightly off. We sat in my father's kitchen and he told me about his math class and I told him about mine, and neither of us mentioned the bar, or the red stools, or the men in feathered boas who called me honey. I went to bed that night having decided that my father's world was something you kept in a drawer, and that boys like Josh lived in the room where the drawer was.

In March, my father went to a doctor. He came home and told me it was nothing, and then he came home and told me it was something, and then he stopped coming home to tell me anything at all and started coming home to sit on the couch with the television on and the volume off. The scans were every six weeks. The oncologist used the word "aggressive," which is a word that means the doctors are being kind. The nurse used the word "terminal," which is the only word she ever said that I heard clearly, because she said it in the hallway, not to my father, and then walked away with her clipboard. He lost weight the way a candle loses wax, all at once, then slowly, then all at once again. By April you could see the waffle iron of his ribs through his shirts, and by May the shirts were his father's shirts, and he wore them with more confidence than I ever managed in my own clothes.

Benny found the cruise. Benny, who had never taken a vacation in his life and once drove four hours to watch a canasta tournament that he lost. He and Ray and Marcus and a handful of others pooled money for cabins, and the ship's marketing department sent the brochure, and my father sat at the kitchen table and looked at it and said, "I'm going." The doctor had told him to go do something stupid, and he said I was the only person on earth he trusted not to treat him like a patient, which was unfair of him and also true, because I had been trained at the register to smile at everything.

The cabin placard on the door read GORDON, which made me realize I had never thought of him by his name at all. Inside were two beds with plastic flowers and a minibar that charged eleven dollars for a bottle of water. The ship smelled of sunscreen and deep-fried bread and the particular nothing-smell of ocean air that has been recycled through vents. The muster drill was a comedy: the captain in his white hat telling four hundred men to find their life jackets in the event of abandonment, and my father singing along to the song they played, off-key, the way he did everything.

Within two days I had stopped being the kid and started being furniture. The men of the Porch spread across the pool deck like a family reunion that had been waiting forty years to happen. Benny wore a feathered boa in the water, which was not a metaphor. Ray read paperbacks under a striped umbrella and never once got a sunburn. Marcus did laps with the seriousness of a man on a mission, and his son Theo, seventeen, lay beside the pool on a lounger with his headphones on, reading the same book he had been reading since before we boarded. The pool deck was hot and loud and full of men I had known my whole life, and I was handed a bag of pool noodles and told to distribute them, and I did, and no one was surprised.

At canasta, the game that Benny played with the ferocity of a man settling an old score, an older man named Frankie asked me what I did with my summers. I said I worked at my father's bar. He said, "The Porch? I know the Porch," and I said, "You're from around here?" and he laughed and said he was from four towns away, which turned out to be true, and then he asked me about boys and girls, gently, the way you ask a weather question. I said I wasn't sure. He said, "Good. You've got time," and I felt, for the first time in my life, that my uncertainty was being held rather than corrected. There were other kids on the ship, a small colony of them, children of the guests, some of them raised in the same world I was, and we clustered around the arcade and the teen lounge and the buffet's chocolate fountain, and I was among them the way I had been among the regulars: a fixture, a regular, someone the place already knew.

I met Theo properly on the third day. He was sitting across from me at the buffet with a plate he wasn't eating, and he said, "Do you know the Wi-Fi password?" and I said, "It's on the cabin card," and he said, "I didn't think of that," and I said, "I didn't think of that either," and he laughed, which was a real laugh, small and surprised, and not the performative laughter of adults at a party. We talked about the ship. He told me the pool was colder than it looked and that the buffet's squid was the worst thing he had ever eaten, and I agreed, and he looked at me as if I had confirmed a theory. That night we walked the promenade while the ship listed through a squall off the Bahamas, the dark water going flat and black under the bow, and he told me he had never been on a ship before and that he had expected to hate it and was surprised to like it, and I said the same thing, and he said, "You're not as weird as your dad's friends," and I said, "That's a high bar," and we both laughed at the railing.

We danced once, at the teen lounge, to a song I didn't recognize, and he stepped on my foot twice, and neither of us commented on it. He asked for my phone number before we got off the ship, and I gave it, and he texted me a few times over the week, short messages: "did you see the squid at the buffet tonight," "the pool is cold," "good luck with canasta," and after we got home the messages stopped, which felt like the correct amount of ending for two strangers who had been friendly for seven days.

The last night the ship threw its farewell party, which meant a disco ball and a dance floor and a DJ who played music from the nineties at a volume that made conversation impossible. My father stood at the rail with his arms folded, watching the deck, and I could see how tired he was, the way the body gets tired when it is fighting a war it isn't winning, and I said, "You should dance," and he said, "I don't dance," and I said, "You dance at the Porch," and he said, "That's not dancing, that's surviving," and then the DJ played Stevie Wonder's "Isn't She Lovely," and my father looked at me, and there was no one else around him, because he had never been married and never had a partner and had spent fifty years with men who danced badly and happily, and so he put his hand on my shoulder and stepped onto the floor, and I put my hand on his back, low, the way he'd shown me at the bar, and we swayed.

He didn't step. He swayed, and his hand tightened on my shoulder, and he mouthed the words, and I could see his ribs through his shirt, and I could feel the weight of him, which was less than it had been in the spring, which was more than it would be in the fall. He said, "See, I told you I could dance." I said, "You can't." He said, "I can if I hold on." Benny was dancing nearby with a boa and a canasta card in his pocket, and Ray was clapping with his thermos, and the whole deck was clapping, and my father was mouthing the words of a song about how lovely a child is, and he was smiling like a man who has been told he can go home whenever he wants and has chosen, instead, to stay.

We got home on the twelfth. He ate an entire plate of pasta at the airport, which Sunny told me later was the kind of thing that worried her more than the scans. The scans got worse in July. In September he went to the hospice house, where they gave him a room with a window facing the strip, so that he could see the Porch's neon if he wanted, and he sat by that window and watched the bar fill and empty, fill and empty, the way it had done for fifty years. In October he died, in his sleep, with Benny's thermos of soup on the table, which was cold by then, and which Ray finished in the parking lot.

The jukebox at the Porch still skips on certain songs. It plays Stevie Wonder fine. I go there sometimes when I need to remember that the world my father lived in was not a drawer but a room, a warm one, full of people who knew his name, and that I had spent my whole life inside it without ever thinking of it as anywhere but home. He would have hated how people describe that night on the ship. He'd have called it a Tuesday. He danced badly and happily, and he held on, and that is the whole story of him.
